articles.title: Saponin extract from Astragalus membranaceus (Fisch.) Bunge regulates gut-brain axis through intestinal Escherichia coli to reduce cerebral oxidative stress to treat vascular dementia in rodents.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Vascular dementia (VD) is a cognitive dysfunction syndrome caused by cerebrovascular diseases. Astragalus membranaceus (Fisch.) Bunge (AS) has antioxidative, gut microbiota-regulating, and cognitive-improving effects. Escherichia coli (E. coli) abundance is associated with cognitive dysfunction. This study explored the mechanism by which AS improves VD by regulating E. coli along the gut-brain axis, providing a basis for VD drug research and development. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: VD models were established by permanent ligation of the common carotid artery. Morris water maze, Doppler cerebral blood flow measurement, blood lipid assays, pathological staining, Western blot, and ELISA were used to evaluate AS's protective effects on the brain. 16S rRNA sequencing analyzed gut microbiota to screen differential strains. Metabolomics screened endogenous differential metabolites. Oxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD) was established to evaluate 5-aminovaleric acid effects on neuronal mitochondrial function and oxidative stress. KEY RESULTS: AS significantly improved cognitive dysfunction, restored cerebral blood flow, and attenuated abnormal protein accumulation and oxidative stress in VD rat brains. Microbiota analysis revealed that AS inhibited E. coli proliferation and mitigated associated pathological damage. Furthermore, endogenous metabolite 5-aminovaleric acid alleviated OGD-induced neuronal damage and oxidative stress. CONCLUSION AND IMPLICATIONS: AS can treat cognitive dysfunction and brain injury in rodents, regulate gut microbiota balance, and reduce the contribution of E. coli. Meanwhile, AS-regulated endogenous metabolite 5-aminovaleric acid can also treat OGD-induced nerve cell injury. These findings suggest that AS may be a promising candidate for VD treatment and provide mechanistic insight into gut-brain axis regulation.

articles.title: Proteomic Profiling of Xenobiotic and Nutrient Transporters in Human Placenta of Different Gestational Ages.
articles.abstract: The placenta serves a critical role in nutrient uptake and waste elimination for the developing fetus. The placenta is also responsible for the uptake and/or exchange of xenobiotics, including medications, between the maternal and fetal bloodstreams. An estimated 40-80% of women take medications or drugs during pregnancy. Very little is understood about fetal drug and nutrient exposure during pregnancy and how it may change over the course of fetal development. This study aimed to characterize the abundance of transport proteins in placental tissue, which are important in modulating fetal nutrient and drug exposure, over the duration of pregnancy. Using a mass spectrometry-based global proteomic approach, the relative abundance of proteins in placental tissue samples was profiled from first trimester, second trimester, and term placenta samples. Our analysis detected a total of 6331 proteins which included a total of 139 solute carrier and ATP-binding cassette transport proteins that were detected across the dataset, and 80 that were quantified in every sample. In general, membrane-associated proteins, including solute carrier and ATP-binding cassette transport proteins, were significantly enriched in placental tissue collected during early gestation compared to term placental tissue. Overall, this study presents a comprehensive profiling of membrane-associated proteomic changes during gestation and identifies significant gestational age associated abundance changes at the protein level in several transport protein families. These data provide critical information to support future studies into the understanding of fetal exposure to xenobiotics and nutrients circulating in the maternal bloodstream.

articles.title: PFAS:VDR interactions and immunotoxicity through disruption of monocyte differentiation.
articles.abstract: Accumulating evidence indicates that per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) have the capacity to modulate vitamin D receptor (VDR) signaling however, the underlying mechanisms governing these interactions remain poorly understood. In the present study, we investigated direct interactions between PFAS and VDR signaling, as well as a novel, putative mechanism by which PFAS may induce immunotoxicity through disruption of VDR molecular functionalities. VDR is widely expressed across both the innate and adaptive branches of the immune system, where it plays critical roles in regulating immune cell activation, differentiation, and function. While PFAS exposure has been consistently associated with immune dysregulation and reduced vaccine responsiveness in both human and animal studies, the molecular basis of PFAS-induced immunotoxicity is only partially defined. To address these knowledge gaps, we examined a panel of PFAS compounds previously identified through computational modeling to possess measurable binding affinities for the VDR. We employed a suite of complementary, orthogonal bioassays to characterize the functional interactions between PFAS and the vitamin D receptor. These included a transient transactivation assay to assess global receptor agonist and antagonist activity, a Mammalian two-Hybrid (M2H) assay to evaluate PFAS effects on VDR interactions with its obligate heterodimerization partner (RXR), coactivator (SRC-1), and corepressor (NCoR1), and a THP-1 cell differentiation/transcription assay to probe the transcriptional consequences of PFAS exposure on vitamin D-facilitated monocyte cell differentiation. Collectively, our findings reveal that select PFAS engage in complex molecular interactions with the VDR and act as potent antagonists, effectively inhibiting vitamin D-mediated receptor function and downstream THP-1 cell signaling.

articles.title: Population pharmacokinetics of levetiracetam in term neonates with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy and therapeutic hypothermia: The LEVNEONAT-1 study.
articles.abstract: AIM: This study aimed to describe the pharmacokinetics (PK) of levetiracetam (LEV) in term neonates treated for neonatal seizures secondary to hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE). METHODS: Fifteen neonates were included and received a loading dose ranging from 30 to 60 mg/kg followed by eight maintenance doses corresponding to one-fourth of the loading dose every 8 h. Five blood PK samples were drawn for each neonate: three after the loading dose and two after the last maintenance dose. Data were analysed by a population approach using NONMEM software. The possible relationship between LEV Cmax and AUC from time 0 to 4 h after the loading dose (AUC4h) and the relative seizure difference (RSD) that defined the LEV efficacy was investigated by linear regression. RESULTS: LEV PK was described by a two-compartment model with allometric scaling based on body weight. Typical values (%IIV) for LEV CL, central and peripheral distribution volume (Vc and Vp) and distribution clearance (Q) were 4.27 (15%) L/h, 46.5 (14%) L, 6.10 L (98%) and 1.75 L/h, respectively. Creatinine clearance (CLcr) and natremia were found to be significant covariates for LEV clearance (CL), CL increasing with CLcr and natremia. No relationship was found between LEV Cmax or AUC4h and RSD. CONCLUSION: A population PK model of LEV in term neonates with HIE was developed. The influence of natremia was highlighted for the first time and could reflect the relationship between the encephalopathy severity and LEV PK in this population.
